title: Warming Doesn't Just Melt Glaciers — It Reshapes Your Brain's Decisions
dek: The brain is a statistical model of its environment, and climate is the human-set baseline for normal. When the baseline itself moves, forgetting becomes an adaptation mechanism — you slide into treating the abnormal as normal without noticing.
why: Medium information density; the core value is in the neural-mechanism framework up front and the policy gap at the back. Worth hearing for anyone interested in the intersection of climate and cognition; skip it if you're purely hunting for investment targets.
who: Founders, investors and policy researchers interested in the intersection of climate and cognition; managers assessing how climate risk affects organizational decisions and employee cognition.
skip: The podcast intro and book recommendations from 0:43-4:54 can be skipped; go straight to 4:54 where the substance starts.

points.h: The brain is a statistical model of its environment, not a hard drive
points.body: Aldern defines the brain as ‘a statistical model of the environment’ — a generative model that lets an organism represent the external world and navigate it successfully. The model's core function is to measure the gap between expectation and actual perception. When a gap appears, the organism has only two paths: update the model to match perception, or take action to change perception. This ‘action-perception loop’ is the foundation for understanding every climate effect that follows. Climate anxiety is only the surface; the real problem is that the model itself is being reshaped by environmental change.

points.h: Climate doesn't exist — it's just a cultural construct
points.body: Aldern makes a counterintuitive claim: climate is not an entity you can reach out and touch. A raindrop landing on your hand is real — that's weather. Climate is ‘the definition of normality for any given point in time and space,’ a human-constructed average — the World Meteorological Organization defines it as a 30-year, 10-kilometer-by-10-kilometer average. In other words, climate is expectation itself. If the brain's core function is calibrating expectation against perception, and climate as expectation is changing, then your nervous system must change along with it.

points.h: Forgetting is an adaptation mechanism, not a cognitive defect
points.body: If the brain is a model and climate is expectation, what happens when the expectation itself is moving? Aldern's answer: forgetting. If you remembered every climatic past, you couldn't adapt to the new world. So ‘we ought to forget what the world currently is not, in order to successfully navigate the new world.’ This produces a paradox: a voice in your ear whispering ‘it's actually always been like this, this is the definition of normal.’ The battle over climate therefore has two fronts — the external physical world, and the external world's remodeling of your internal representation.

points.h: Heat unbalances the prefrontal cortex, and vmPFC takes over decisions
points.body: From heated telegraph operators in a 1940s Cambridge lab to 1980s psychology labs, research has consistently found: under heat people are more impulsive, less rational, less capable of critical thinking. The mechanism is that brain tissue is extremely sensitive to temperature and must burn extra metabolic energy to cool down. That crowds out fixed attentional resources. Concretely in neuroscience terms: the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) handles critical thinking, while the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) receives emotional input from the amygdala and elsewhere. In a healthy environment the two are balanced; under extreme heat the DLPFC overloads, the vmPFC takes over, and decisions become impulsive.

points.h: Heat increases violence: from car horns to retaliatory hit-by-pitches
points.body: In the 1980s researchers hid in bushes to watch how the car behind reacted when the car ahead didn't move after the light turned green. In hot weather, especially in vehicles with open windows (suggesting no air conditioning), honking increased, horn presses lasted longer, and drivers were more likely to swear. The effect extends into professional domains: baseball pitchers are more likely to throw retaliatory pitches in the heat; a Harvard economist's study of harassment complaints in the postal system found that the hotter it was, the more harassment — for both indoor and outdoor workers. Online hate speech, domestic violence and interpersonal violence all rise with relative temperature deviation.

points.h: Blue-green algae neurotoxins may travel through the air
points.body: Cyanobacteria produce the neurotoxin BMAA, known to be associated with ALS, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. The new finding is that BMAA may spread via aerosols, so people living around lakes may also be exposed. Warming drives cyanobacteria blooms from three directions: synthetic fertilizer runoff balances the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio, warmer water temperatures, and extreme storms washing more fertilizer into rivers. Globally, cyanobacteria blooms are increasing in both scale and frequency. Aldern warns: if cyanobacteria are everywhere at a global scale, they could cause serious damage in the coming decades.

points.h: In-utero hurricane exposure means ten times the depression risk at six
points.body: Research on the Paradise fire shows PTSD risk stratification: people who neither lost property nor directly experienced the fire were basically normal; those who knew someone who lost property or witnessed the event had about three times the PTSD rate; those who themselves lost property or family members were three times higher again. After Hurricane Katrina, roughly half of low-income parents had PTSD symptoms. More striking still is Yoko Nomura's research on Hurricane Sandy: children exposed to the hurricane in utero were ten to twenty times more likely than unexposed children to show anxiety, depression, OCD, ADHD and other cognitive-behavioral deficits by age six. Aldern thinks this hints at epigenetic mechanisms at work.

points.h: Every neural climate effect is still sitting on the shelf, outside policy
points.body: Aldern points to a key gap: a few intergovernmental bodies now seriously consider climate change and health, but large climate policy cost-benefit analyses rarely incorporate those organizations' recommendations. No climate-and-health literature has attempted to price the presenteeism and absenteeism caused by rising workplace temperatures. All the neural effects discussed ‘are sitting on the shelf, existing in conversations like this one, but they haven't yet become part of the policy-making infrastructure.’ He argues that societal-level awareness means integrating well-understood research into the actual decision protocols for governing climate change.
